images.filename: The Archer King, National Museum of Sudan, Khartoum, Sudan, North-East Africa (cropped).jpg
images.caption:
The Archer King, National Museum of Sudan, Khartoum, Sudan, North-East Africa (cropped)
Found at Tabo, on the island of Argo, in a hiding place in the temple. Originally this bronze statue was entirely covered with gold leaf. It represents an unknown Meroitic king (no cartouche was preserved). He wears the traditional crown of the kings of Kush - a cap with two cobras on the forehead - and a necklace with rams' heads on each end. Probably 3rd century BCE, a masterpiece of the period.

images.filename: Temple statue of god Arensnuphis, from Meroe, Nubia (modern-day Sudan), 100-50 BCE. Sandstone. National Museum of Scotland, Edinburgh, Scotland, UK.jpg
images.caption: Temple statue of god Arensnuphis, from Meroe, Nubia (modern-day Sudan), 100-50 BCE. Sandstone. National Museum of Scotland, Edinburgh, Scotland, UK. The statue stood at the entrance into a temple dedicated to the goddess Isis. Found by Professor John Garstang (of the University of Liverpool) during his excavations of the Nibuan city Meroe between 1909-1914 CE.

images.caption: Tobilleras de bronce macizo con decoración incisa de motivos de motivos geométricos. Suelen aparecer en los tobillos del difunto. Su usoy funcionalidad puedeverseen representación de paredes de tumbas y templos meroítico; así en el templo de Apedemak en Naga, cerca de Meroe, aparecen divinidades llevando estas piezas como elementos de adorno tanto en tobillos como en brazos. Época meroítica. 300 a. C.-350 d. C. Nerópolis de Nag el-Arab, tumba 585, Argín (Nubia, Sudán)
